source.title: Different Paths to Harmful Compliance: Behavioral Side Effects and Mechanistic Divergence Across LLM Jailbreaks

record.file_problem: The text includes the main paper and supplementary material and is not cut off. The supplied TITLE differs from the title printed in the text, which is “Behind Harmful Compliance: Behavioral and Mechanistic Divergence Across LLM Jailbreaks.” Some equations and figures are flattened, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests refusal-direction suppression through a harmful–benign activation contrast and weight-space orthogonalization, and tests one-dimensional refusal-direction repair. Its weight-edit intervention and behavioral measures are related to, but not the same as, projecting the direction out of every layer and position or adding it to induce refusal.
record.gate_note: The study directly tests harmful compliance after abliteration and reports capability, self-audit, safety-reflection, and refusal-repair results. It also compares SFT and RLVR. Values used to select layers or other hyperparameters are not included as outcome rows. Category-specific RLVR, PERSIST, and most representation-similarity results are not catalogued here because they do not directly test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study builds a difference-in-means refusal direction from harmful and harmless prompts and applies it as a weight orthogonalization (Arditi et al. recipe) to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. It measures harmful compliance, capability retention and repair by restoring the direction coefficient, which bears on V1 and V2. Its refusal-projection and repair results for harmful RLVR and SFT also bear on V3 for parameter-level jailbreaks. This differs from the original's every-layer projection and activation addition, so the tranche is T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add the mechanistic findings: abliteration nearly removes the base refusal projection and is strongly repaired by restoring it, RLVR keeps much of it and is only partly repaired, and SFT is not repaired. Harmful compliance, harm recognition and capability awareness are separable.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a harmful–benign mean-activation contrast and suppresses it by orthogonalizing selected writer weights at a model-specific mid-to-late layer. It does not test projecting out the direction at every layer and position or adding it to harmless prompts. The study also uses one-dimensional activation patching for repair.
record.method_sensitivity: Effects vary by model family and route. The paper reports family-dependent capability costs and abliteration effects; the true-direction repair sweep varies layer and patch strength, but the text does not give numeric sensitivity results for those sweep settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful-RLVR models comply under direct prompting, yet give base-comparable explicit ratings of policy violation, should-refuse and actionable harm. Reflection prompting cuts their harmfulness from 5.00 to 1.00 (Qwen) and 2.70 (Llama).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning jailbreaks can leave explicit harm recognition intact while disabling refusal behavior; a behavioral analogue of harm/refusal separation.

record.problems: The authors report only two instruction-tuned models and no replications across training seeds. The SFT and RLVR training parameters are not fully matched; RLVR uses an LLM judge whose rewards may contain errors. The paper says CKA, RSA, and one-dimensional refusal-direction patching are descriptive and partly oracle-based. Several relevant results are shown only in figures without recoverable exact values, and no error bars or confidence intervals are stated.
record.rows_left_out: To remain within 60 rows, omitted the remaining Table A2 truthfulness/social-behavior metric rows and Table A3 ETHICS metric rows, as well as PERSIST, most representation-similarity results, and category-specific RLVR transfer results. The selected A2/A3 rows capture notable reported differences; the omitted tables are in Supplementary Sections B and C, Tables A2–A3. Figure-only controls and broader route comparisons are also not separately catalogued.

untested.parts: Projection at every layer and position (only selected writer weights are edited at one layer); adding the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal; over-refusal on harmless prompts.
Community or released abliterated checkpoints beyond the authors' own edits of two 7–8B models.
Prompt-based jailbreaks (GCG and similar); training against ablation for robustness.
Not tested; affine and cone alternatives are only cited.
No representation-level separation of harmfulness and refusal directions.

missing.what: Normalized base-direction margin (hh-hb along base refusal direction) per route. Abliteration nearly removes it; RLVR retains much; SFT less.
True-direction repair scores for RLVR (partial) and SFT (none), needed as rows for the V3 label.
Random-direction control results for the repair patching (described in the methods, values not reported).
Abliterated-model self-audit: intermediate degradation in Qwen, near ceiling in Llama. Harm recognition survives refusal-direction removal in Llama, which is relevant to V5.
Abliterated models under safety reflection: moderate reduction in Qwen, larger in Llama.
Aligned-base harmfulness values for Figure 2 (about 1.0–1.6 in the flattened text), needed as baselines for the abliteration harm rows.
Remaining abliteration rows in Tables A2–A3: Qwen TruthfulQA 62.9→60.2, BBQ 77.2→79.8, ETHICS commonsense 72.3→68.1.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. V5 is not tested at the representation level: the self-audit rows are behavioral, from deliberately trained RLVR models, so they are moved to fits_no_version. Many values are figure-only, with no error bars, two models and one seed. The authors call one-dimensional patching descriptive and partly oracle-based.

versions.untested_parts: Tests removal through weight editing on two instruct models, but not projection at every layer and position, adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests, or a comprehensive assessment of all other abilities.
Tests the study’s abliteration weight edit on two instruct models. It does not establish effects in a sample of released models beyond these checkpoints.
Does not test whether jailbreak attacks work by suppressing the direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not test whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or supported by multiple directions. One-dimensional repair results alone do not test these alternatives.
Compares explicit safety judgments with harmful compliance and tests safety-reflection prompting, but does not directly establish separate internal encodings with a causal representation-level test.
Does not test cross-language transfer, transfer between model variants, or transfer from base to instruct models.
Compares harmful SFT and RLVR jailbreak training, not how or when safety refusal is trained or whether that determines existence of a removable direction.
